The first I would like to ask you about is sources of prosecution witnesses, because I do not want to leave you testifying to the Chamber with the impression that the sole source of witnesses were provided through the AID. Let me ask you, Mr. Leach, were witnesses identified by a variety of sources to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that include witnesses being identified through non-governmental organisations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it include witnesses being identified to the Office of the Prosecutor through the statements of other witnesses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it include the testimony -- did it include the identity of witnesses through UN organisations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it include the identification of witnesses through other sources?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now if I could have Prosecutor's exhibit number 60, Mr. Dubuisson, given to the witness, which is a photo album of the Busovaca mosque. (Handed) All right. Mr. Leach, you were asked on cross-examination a question about the destruction of the minaret. You were shown defence Exhibit 12 and a sentence was highlighted in that. It says and I quote: "Last month Croatian Bosnian forces demolished the minaret of the Busovaca mosque". Does a mosque -- first of all, what is a minaret?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The minaret is the tower-type building which is used by the priest to call worshippers to prayer at various times of the day using a small room and sometimes with a loudhailer or a microphone at the top of the minaret.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does a mosque consist of more than a minaret?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the minaret is a small, round towered structure which is attached to the side of the mosque.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you refer to exhibit number 60, Mr. Leach, and would you take out photograph Z1/788? Place that on the ELMO, please. Now in that particular photograph, Mr. Leach, does it show where the minaret that was destroyed once stood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Where the minaret would have been from the base, and if it was undestroyed, it would have been in this location here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now would you -- in the foreground of that picture, is there a portion of the minaret that's shown?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are pointing now to rubble that's in the foreground; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That would be where the top of the minaret would have been.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now will you please place on the ELMO Z1/869? Mr. Leach, I take it that that photograph is not a photograph of a minaret; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's the mosque. The minaret would have been to the right here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Does that picture clearly show the destruction of the mosque main building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now would you take the next photograph in that series, which was Z1/874? Place that on the ELMO, please. What does that picture depict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's the inside of the main mosque, the main building of the mosque.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that picture taken?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were there, Mr. Leach, was there extensive vegetation growing inside the area of destruction, inside the main mosque?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It's visible inside on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that include small trees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there's one there on the left of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now the last area -- you can reassemble that exhibit, before I get to my last area of enquiry. Mr. Leach, you were asked some questions about Colonel Bob Stewart's book and when he was aware of the events in Ahmici. Were you aware -- are you aware that British soldiers were in Ahmici on 16th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Those were subordinates of Colonel Stewart; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I have no further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Riad, have you any questions you would like to ask? Yes. Judge Riad would like to ask the witness some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Leach, you have shown us different pictures of the destruction which happened in the villages and which you saw on the ground. Could these destructions be the result of war and fighting, an inevitable result? Could the result -- could the destruction of the minaret especially, which you have just shown us, be just a result of this fighting or was it a deliberate -- it could be a deliberate destruction? Were they deliberate targets to be destroy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was visiting these locations, your Honour, I had with me several military officers as escorts of a variety of disciplines, infantry, helicopter pilots, etc. I'm not a military expert, so what I'm telling you now is based on what they told me. Each of the mosques that I've shown photographs of, as you walk into the mosque, you can walk on to what I call a first floor balcony. The minaret is always to the right of the entrance. It appears that some kind of explosive charge, whether that is specifically put together as an explosive charge or whether it's the use, for example, which was suggested to me at the time, of a large anti-tank mine, then that would be detonated, this charge, and the minaret would then tumble down. It does not appear to be the result of shelling. For each minaret to have had the same point of detonation, to have fallen over in the same manner, the shelling would have been unbelievably accurate. It does appear to be deliberate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: In this route distancing which was given to us, one can see that most of the villages were within minutes from Vitez, from Hotel Vitez. Ahmici was within seven minutes by car and 4 kms. Others were within four minutes. Others were within six minutes, five minutes by car. Is this distance enough to make it possible for anyone in Vitez to be aware of the explosions happening around, or even to see through technical means or through field glasses, to see what's happening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again I can only give evidence, hearsay or opinion evidence, but I think you will hear evidence from other witnesses and you will see additional evidence where it is quite clear that, for example, plumes of smoke from a variety of burning houses are quite clearly visible over distances in excess of 3 and 4 kms. Witnesses have told me, you know, that one could hear the sounds of explosions 4, 5 and 6 kms away. So the answer to your question, your Honour, is yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Leach. I myself would like to ask Mr. Harmon a question. I'm turning to you, Mr. Harmon, because you are heading the team. These are the conditions for application of Rule 70 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. I would like you to tell the Trial Chamber exactly under Rule 70 in relation to the aerial photographs, and once you have explained the conditions in which you find yourself in relation to this article, I would like to know whether you had other sources and whether all the sources were disclosed to the accused as shown -- as required by Rule 70B. Could you answer that question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If you give me just a moment to look at Rule 70B, your Honour ... (Pause.)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: My colleagues have pointed out to me that we are talking about the use of Rule 70 for initial information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Are you asking me whether we had received this information initially for purposes of generating new evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: There are three conditions. It is initial information which should be obtained only for gathering new evidence, and you need the consent of the person or the entity. Here it is the British Ministry of Defence. This is a consequence rather than a condition. The information condition be used as evidence before having disclosed it to the Defence, which is a sub question which I'm asking having to do with the number of maps which were supplied to the Defence and which are now being tendered as exhibits. Was this all disclosed to the Defence before this hearing?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, your Honour. One photograph was; the remaining photographs were not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that we have now completed the testimony of Simon Leach. The Tribunal would like to thank you. We have just decided that you should remain available both to the accused, but to the Defence as well, which is a request which came from the Defence and which was granted by the Trial Chamber. You may now return to your duties. We turn to the Prosecutor for the following witness. Thank you very much. (Witness withdraws from court)

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President and your Honours. The Prosecutor calls Sefkija Djidic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Perhaps counsel could spell that name, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Which is exactly what my colleague asked and I was going to ask myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The last name, your Honour, is Djidic, D-J-I-D-I-C. Sefkija, S-E-F-K-I-J-A. Many Bosniaks in Bosnia will refer to their last name first and often refer to themselves as "Djidic Sefkija" when their family name is Djidic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Therefore it is Mr. Djidic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. (Witness enters court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, do you hear me? First of all, I would like to ask whether you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please read the statement or the declaration which was given to you, read it in your language, please. Mr. Sefkija Djidic (sworn) Examined by Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: May I proceed, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, proceed please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sir, can you please state your name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am Sefkija Djidic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, how old are you and where do you live?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm 43 and I live in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, tell us a little bit about yourself personally, your background, where you are from originally, where you have lived during your 43 years. If you could provide that to the Tribunal, it would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in Vitez. I completed elementary and secondary school in Vitez. I graduated from the University in Sarajevo. After gradation I worked in a secondary school as a teacher for about four years. After that I started working in a military factory as the chief of protocol for the admission of foreign guests. After five or six years I was appointed head of a department and that is the security department for the military facility. I worked there until May 1992. In May 1992 I joined the Territorial Defence. After that I worked as chief of staff of the Territorial Defence, and in August I was appointed commander of the Territorial Defence of Vitez. In the course of 1992 I engaged in preparations and the deployment of Territorial Defence units for defence against aggression. The conflict with the Croats in 1993 occurred when I was in Stari Vitez, where I stayed for all of 11 months under encirclement. After the conflict, after the truce was signed in February 1994, I was reunited with my family and I left to live in Travnik, as my house in the conflicts with the HVO was destroyed and my family displaced, my father was killed, and several relatives. I am now temporarily residing in Travnik. I have more or less reconstructed my house in Vitez and I hope to be able to return to my backyard soon. If it's necessary, I'm at your disposal for any further information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, what do you do for work right now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am now working as head of the police station in Vitez. Of course, in the section that is under the control of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as in Vitez there are still two police stations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the town of Vitez as of July 1997 essentially separated between a Bosnian Croat and a Bosnian Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is still divided.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, would it be fair to tell this court that except for the period of time when you were studying at the University of Sarajevo, you have spent essentially your entire life living around the Vitez area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your time, sir, as an adult, were you ever part of the military, the former Yugoslav people's army, as a military officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the President and the judges exactly what your military experience was and is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to do my military service in a military school for officers in reserve of the former JNA. In 1972 I attended the school for reserve officers in Bileca and after completing this training, I acquired the rank of Reserve Lieutenant of the former JNA. In the period from 1973 until 1990 I attended several specialisation courses and held responsible positions of command. More recently I was commander of a partisan battalion. These were mobile units of the reserve units. The highest rank I acquired was in 1990, when the rank was Captain first class.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you achieve this rank, Mr. Djidic, when you were a reserve officer as opposed to an active duty officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as a reserve officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And while you were a reserve officer, did you continue to work in the SPS factory, as you described before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I and all other reserve officers and troops engaged in our normal duties, and we would be called up occasionally to attend exercises, various training courses, seminars and camping periods, depending on what we were supposed to learn. At the end of an exercise all the reserve officers and soldiers would go back to their factories and to their regular jobs, and would continue working and living as civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Djidic, I would like to take your testimony in three separate segments, the first segment dealing with the build-up of the conflict, the second segment the conflict itself, and the third segment, the seizure. Starting with the first segment, Mr. Djidic, could you tell the court exactly what life was like in Bosnia and the Lasva Valley prior to the outbreak of hostilities? Was it a good life, a bad life?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I will talk about that gladly. Life in Bosnia and in Yugoslavia was a very good life. When talking about Bosnia, especially Central Bosnia, which we are now actually dealing with, our life was almost ideal from the standpoint of cohabitation. I grew up in a settlement which was inhabited by both Serbs, Croats and Muslims. Never did we have any major problems. Simply we lived like a big extended family. These were mostly original inhabitants, old timers, people who knew each other for many years. They visited one another frequently. They went to each other's homes for any celebrations and in events of sadness. We would visit one another for religious events and festivities and the children particularly rejoiced when Bijram would come, Easter or Christmas, when children would be given cookies, coloured eggs, roast meat, and the adults would sit together and feast on delicacies. That was a custom observed by all three sides. We grew up together. We went to school together. We engaged in sports together. All in all everything we did, we did together. Only our religious places of worship were separate, as is normal. There were churches and there were mosques, which were visited by people belonging to the respective ethnic groups. It was not rare for a member of another ethnic group to visit the place of worship of another group. This was mostly out of curiosity, one must say, but also it was prompted by the desire to attend large rallies, when a large number of young people were present, good looking young men and pretty girls. Also it was not uncommon for religious events, or to be more precise, meetings or festivities to be attended by a certain number of young men and women belonging to a different ethnic group, again out of the curiosity, but also in order to get to know one another. This kind of socialising resulted in the formation of mixed marriages, which were very numerous in Vitez, combining members of all three groups. At one point in time you simply didn't know when you pronounce somebody's name which religion or nation he belonged to, and I can assure you that I am happy to have lived in such an environment. I hope that that life will be restored.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, when did things begin to change in Vitez and Central Bosnia; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Things started to change in the course of the preparations for the elections. That was in 1990, when there were first isolated cases of people acting and speaking according to their ethnic origin, and as time went by this became increasingly frequent and more widespread.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Taking it on from there, was there some identification with political parties by each ethnic side in the elections of 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: More or less, yes, a majority of people, but not all. All the people in Vitez did not join national parties. This can be said of Croats, of Serbs and Muslims. There were people who opted for parties which were not nationally coloured, and one might say that in most cases those were people from mixed marriages, and especially people that had constant contact with people of different ethnic backgrounds. Unfortunately there were not too many of those people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, after the election of 1990, were there other events that caused a raising of tensions between the various ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. A struggle for power ensued. Simply with the disintegration of the communist system each of the parties had their own programmes, which, when studied closely, were good and constructive. There was little difference among them, because not one of those programmes envisaged war. However, later on one could read between the lines and gather from that, and that is what in effect happened, that there were people who wanted to capture Bosnia and Herzegovina and to proclaim it to be their state alone. In the first case this applied to the Serbs, who carried out an aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina, and, secondly, it was the extreme section of Croats who at that time tried to and actually succeeded in forming the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, which later acquired the outlines of a State within a State. From that moment on, when the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was formed, even greater problems presented themselves, especially for the Muslims, who were already defending themselves from the Serbs' aggression.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go back to the formation of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Mr. Djidic, do you recall approximately when the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was formed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was in 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the relationship between the Bosnian Muslims in the Vitez area and the Bosnian Croats change after the formation of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Relations changed substantially. This was evidenced by various phenomena and in various places, where the Muslims became second rate in relation to the Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Explain that, Mr. Djidic. What do you mean when you say that "Muslims became second rate in relation to the Bosnian Croats"? Could you explain that to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, the political leadership of the HDZ wanted everyone in the so-called Herceg-Bosna to observe the laws of Herceg-Bosna and to recognise the authority of Herceg-Bosna, that is of the Croats, regardless of whether there were 100, 1,000 or many thousand Muslims living in a particular town, that is to say in Vitez, where the ratio in terms of the population was more or less 50: 50, with only 2 or 3 per cent -- with the Croats having only 2 or 3 per cent higher share in the population. As a second reason and explanation that the Muslims became second rate, I would like to refer to the fact that workers, Muslims, who did not wish to sign their allegiance to Herceg-Bosna were fired by their employers. A further interesting example is the fact that with the formation of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the Croats placed flags on all institutions and factories and even private homes, flags which were those of a neighbouring state, that is The Republic of Croatia, that is the national flag, as if no-one else lived in Vitez except the Croats. There are many more examples that one might refer to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Djidic, you said that there were elections in 1990 throughout Bosnia. Were the Muslims in the Vitez area or any place else in Central Bosnia given a choice as to whether or not they wanted their particular opstina or municipality to become a part of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you -- I'm sorry. Continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time of the elections each individual was free to choose one of the parties. The aim and task of each party was to come into power. However, that power would be a joint -- a joint government would be established, which would be shared in percentages, as emerged from the elections, so that all the people living in the territory of the Vitez municipality would be represented in that government, and that would have been correct, if it had been done that way. However, it was not done that way. The HDZ wanted through the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna to control all power and to be superior, to have control over all people who lived in the -- within the imagined borders of Herceg-Bosna. Similarly the authorities of the so-called Herceg-Bosna did not recognise the legally elected authorities in the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina based in Sarajevo, but had their own supreme authority, which in those days was situated in Grude and in Mostar, or, to be more precise, in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that the authorities in Vitez for the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna would not recognise the authority of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is common knowledge to me and everyone else, because HDZ representatives did not go for consultations to Sarajevo, but went for consultations to Grude, to Mostar and to Zagreb. Simply the man who was at the time President of the Presidency was not recognised as the legitimate representative of all the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was that individual?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, the President of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now did have you conversations with HDZ political leaders in Vitez who told you that they would not recognise the authority of President Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The meetings that we had and which were very frequent with HDZ members and members of the HVO were mostly held over the establishment and recognition of the authority of the HVO, as the only possible solution for these parts of the imagined Herceg-Bosna. On one occasion Mr. Pero Skopljak at a meeting attended by -- still attended by both Muslims and Croats said that he did not recognise Alija or the army, but that his authority in Grude was -- that his authorities were in Grude and in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, who were these other political leaders besides Pero Skopljak and what was Pero Skopljak's role?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pero Skopljak initially, that is in 1991, was the chief of police and at the same time I think he was the President of the HDZ. That is why he gave up his post as chief of police and dedicated himself to the work of the Presidency of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just going back to my question, Mr. Djidic, could you identify the other political leaders of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and the HDZ? Who over the course of time indicated to you that they were not going to comply with the laws of The Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Vitez people, Croats, with whom I had contact most frequently and who were also the authors together with people from other cities of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna were in the first place: Ivicia Santic, Anto Valenta, Pero Skopljak, Marjan Skopljak, Mario Cerkez and many others, together with Mr. Kordic, who was from Busovaca, but who at that time was one of the leaders of the party of the Croatian Democratic Union, as well as Mate Boban, whom I did not have occasion to talk to, but people from Vitez mostly had to be given advice and to receive orders from the authorities that were based in Grude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, Mr. Kehoe, I think we'll stop for today. I would like to remind you that we'll resume for a closed hearing on Monday at 9.30, and we will then resume the questioning of Mr. Djidic at 2.30 on Monday. The court stands adjourned. (1.00 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: --ooOoo-- 25
